executive_assessment.text: Iraq's most consequential climate-development risk is a compound water-heat-agriculture problem whose severity depends as much on institutions, infrastructure, demand and transboundary management as on the physical climate signal.

Climate-FCV interactions are credibly documented as mediated and localized, especially through water competition, livelihood loss, mobility, service pressure and unequal resource/assistance governance; the evidence does not support a deterministic national climate-conflict claim.
Iraq has growing formal adaptation capacity, but evaluated evidence of implementation effectiveness remains substantially thinner than evidence of plans, financing and institutional architecture.

coverage.gap_note: Exposure maps and fine-scale population overlays remain thin.
Limited quantitative comparison among gender, disability and minority groups.
Evidence comes from a small number of localities.
Outcomes are mostly modeled or planned.
Effective authority, financing and implementation quality remain less documented.
Few evaluations directly test climate-adaptation outcomes.
Causal identification is weak; local findings cannot be nationalized.

coverage.value: heat, drought, rainfall variability, flood, dust, salinity
coverage.gap_note: Attribution and future dust/salinity projections remain thin.
Marsh-specific and hydropower projections need additional primary evidence.
Differentiated impacts require stronger household-level quantitative evidence.

coverage.value: conflict legacies, infrastructure, contamination, service delivery
coverage.gap_note: Attribution of specific service failures to conflict versus chronic underinvestment is rarely quantified.

coverage.value: federal, regional, governorate, municipal, basin and community capacity
coverage.gap_note: Municipal and basin-level implementation performance is unevenly studied.

coverage.value: evaluated response effectiveness and unintended effects
coverage.gap_note: Major adaptation programmes such as SRVALI are too new for outcome evaluation.

geographic_notes.text: Evidence should not be read as spatially uniform. Physical projections distinguish the hotter/drier northern highlands, western/central areas and Southern Mesopotamian Plain, while the KRI Local Adaptation Plan pertains only to the Kurdistan Region.

The strongest direct Climate-FCV examples are localized. Berghof covers only Makhmur, Tal Afar and Al-Rifai; UNAMI's Dhi Qar, Missan, Muthanna, Basra, Kirkuk and other examples are selected qualitative cases rather than a representative national sample.

Southern Iraq has particularly visible water, salinity, agricultural and climate-displacement pressures; central and northern urban areas also face service and water-rationing pressures. Federal Iraq and the Kurdistan Region have distinct institutional arrangements and should not be collapsed into a single delivery-capacity finding. (The United Nations in Iraq)

Conflict-affected return areas require separate treatment because damaged infrastructure, displacement history and armed-actor influence create adaptation constraints not necessarily present elsewhere. UNDP's independent evaluation sampled several northern, central and southern areas but cancelled planned visits to Kirkuk, Sulaymaniyah and Najaf because of security/visa constraints.

Important underrepresented populations/areas include smaller climate-displaced groups outside established registration systems, highly insecure or politically inaccessible locations, some marsh communities, persons with disabilities, informal urban settlements and communities for which gender/ethnicity-disaggregated climate outcomes are unavailable.

sector_notes.text: *Well covered: water resources and WASH; agriculture and food security; displacement/mobility; institutional climate planning; conflict-sensitive natural-resource governance.
*Moderately covered: labour/heat exposure, social protection, urban service delivery, ecosystem planning and conflict-damaged infrastructure. (World Bank)

*Thin or absent: quantified future health burdens, electricity-system climate reliability, hydropower-specific risk, transport impacts, marsh restoration effectiveness, dust-storm attribution/projections, private-sector adaptation performance and evaluated municipal adaptation outcomes.

known_gaps.text: Climate-projection gap. Temperature evidence is comparatively robust, but precipitation and hydrological projections are materially more uncertain. There is insufficient primary evidence here to quantify future drought, flood, dust-storm and salinity risk consistently across all governorates.

Attribution gap. Water scarcity reflects climate, structural aridity, upstream management, demand growth, domestic allocation, pollution, infrastructure and operational choices. The evidence does not provide a defensible percentage attribution to each driver.

Climate-FCV causal gap. Direct violence examples exist, but most climate-security literature is qualitative, correlational or pathway-based. It cannot establish a national marginal causal effect of climate stress on violence.

Geographic/population gap. Local studies cover a small subset of districts and governorates. Conflict-affected or hard-to-access areas, informal settlements, PWDs and several minority populations remain weakly represented.

Differentiated-vulnerability gap. National policy clearly identifies women, youth, rural populations and persons with disabilities, but comparative quantitative evidence measuring their different climate losses, coping resources and adaptation outcomes is insufficient.

Evaluation and unintended-effect gap. Formal adaptation investment is expanding, but major programmes generally provide theories of change, beneficiary targets or planned outputs rather than independently evaluated climate-resilience outcomes. Existing independent evaluations concern broader UNDP/WFP portfolios. (The United Nations in Iraq)

FCV-to-climate evidence gap. Armed-actor influence, conflict legacies and weak governance are credibly linked to poorer resource management and service delivery, but the magnitude of their effect on adaptation outcomes is rarely measured.

Mobility-data gap. A current UN synthesis provides September 2025 climate-displacement totals, but classifications can combine climate and broader environmental factors, and consistent longitudinal evidence connecting hazard, livelihood change, movement, destination and subsequent conflict outcomes remains limited. (The United Nations in Iraq)

Access/verification gap. The official WFP evaluation publication page was accessible, but its full report was not retrievable through the browsing environment and the page's displayed publication date conflicts with its stated evaluation coverage period. Its conclusions are therefore used cautiously and the date is not asserted as verified. (World Food Programme)

*None completely absent, but coping-capacity, adaptive-capacity, response-performance and resilience-peace-capacity are only partially covered because the available evidence is localized, plan-based, modeled or not climate-specific in evaluation design.
